title: Can We Settle for Assimilation?
author: Harriett Janetos
summary: Harriett Janetos applies Jim Hewitt and Nidhi Sachdeva's research on why evidence fails to change professional minds to the science-of-reading debate, arguing that presenting balanced-literacy and whole-language teachers with evidence for foundational-skills instruction rarely works because those teachers experience the change not as a neutral methods update but as a threat to deeply held identity and values. Drawing on the psychological distinction between assimilation (fitting new information into an existing framework) and accommodation (reorganizing the framework itself), she proposes a deliberately incremental strategy: rather than demanding the harder accommodation immediately, show teachers how explicit foundational-skills instruction can be assimilated into their existing, genuinely correct value of prioritizing meaningful reading, reframing it as a different vehicle for the same destination rather than a repudiation of it. Her key move is disentangling instructional methods from the values they have become symbolically fused to, citing Zach Groshell's essay reordering its own three key points to lead with reassurance, and arguing the real problem is not that balanced-literacy teachers' values are wrong but that an ineffective method (the three-cueing system) has come to symbolize a value (access to meaningful books) that a different method (automatic word recognition) can actually deliver. She closes with concrete professional-development guidance: elicit teachers' existing beliefs explicitly rather than assuming blank slates, and separate instructional methods from the educational values they have become fused to before presenting new evidence.
points: Janetos's reframe of the science-of-reading conflict is genuinely novel among reform advocates: rather than asking balanced-literacy teachers to abandon their core value (reading meaningful books matters), she proposes showing them how foundational-skills instruction can be assimilated as a different vehicle for that same value, deliberately postponing the harder cognitive work of accommodation.

Her diagnosis of why the debate stalls is precise: 'certain ineffective instructional approaches, like a misapplication of the three-cueing system, have come to symbolize those values,' so questioning the method gets experienced as questioning the underlying value itself, a symbolic fusion that has to be deliberately broken apart.

The concrete professional-development technique she proposes, 'separate instructional methods from educational values... openly affirm them. Then turn to the evidence' — gives teacher-educators an actual sequencing move rather than just a diagnosis of resistance.

Citing Zach Groshell's essay reordering its own three key points to lead with reassurance ('explicit instruction is not a teacher monologue... or a risk to children's self-esteem'), Janetos shows how the order of presenting evidence, not just its content, determines whether threatened values get triggered before the evidence can even be heard.
quotes: We do not evaluate new evidence in isolation. We interpret it through the understandings we already possess, sometimes reshaping new ideas so that they fit our existing thinking. The result may be a distorted understanding, or a conclusion quite different from the one intended, write Jim Hewitt and Nidhi Sachdeva in Why Good Evidence Sometimes Fails to Change Our Minds.
Simply presenting compelling evidence is rarely enough to change professional thinking. Genuine conceptual change requires something more.

Whenever possible, we tend to assimilate rather than accommodate. Assimilation preserves the coherence of what we already believe, whereas accommodation requires us to reorganize our existing understanding, a process that is often considerably more difficult.

These teachers have justifiably elevated the text by placing it front and center in their classrooms, but they may need to be shown how foundational skills instruction supports rather than supplants that focus. The value remains, but the vehicle to develop it changes.

The problem is not with the values balanced literacy teachers hold, which most educators endorse; the problem is that certain ineffective instructional approaches, like a misapplication of the three-cueing system, have come to symbolize those values.

The challenge for teacher educators is to disentangle values from the methods with which they have become associated. The question is not whether values like curiosity, equity, creativity, or learner agency matter, they do. Openly affirm them. Then turn to the evidence and examine which instructional approaches are most likely to achieve these goals in particular instructional contexts, and why.
